title: Chromatin-level readout of the stored state (ATAC/CUT&Tag/Hi-C time courses)
description: After transient stimulation, profile AP-1 motif accessibility, AP-1 occupancy, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at enhancers over time, comparing naive, primed, and recovered cells. Then perturb AP-1 binding acutely, for example with degron-tagged Jun or Fos, at different delays after the stimulus. If memory is stored in the enhancer state and needs AP-1 to be maintained, then late removal should erase it. If AP-1 only writes the state, then late removal should leave it intact, which separates writer from maintainer roles.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use inducible degrons (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after memory is established, then assay whether memory-associated accessibility and gene expression persist without AP-1, distinguishing initiating from maintaining roles.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing/live reporters
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC, or live AP-1 activity reporters tracked through cell divisions, to see whether the memory state is inherited by daughter cells. Test for heterogeneity and bistability in AP-1 activity and accessibility.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge, mapped by ATAC/CUT&RUN
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TGF-β, or inflammatory signal), withdraw it for days to weeks, then re-stimulate. Compare chromatin accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, and transcription at primed versus naive cells to see whether AP-1-bound sites stay open and give a faster or stronger second response.

title: Synthetic optogenetic AP-1 activation with sufficiency testing
description: Drive AP-1 factors (e.g., FOS/JUN) with light-inducible or pulsed expression at varied dose, duration, and frequency, then measure persistence of target gene expression and chromatin changes. Testing whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to create a lasting state, and how pulse patterns affect it, tests its causal role and tunability as a memory mechanism.

title: Targeted motif and site-specific causal editing
description: Mutate or delete specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers with CRISPR base editing, or use dCas9 to block them. Alternatively, use a massively parallel reporter assay or an integrated reporter to test whether enhancer priming and the memory response depend on those motifs. This tests whether the effect is local and sequence-specific, and whether it requires cofactors such as BAF/SWI-SNF, which can be tested by inhibiting them.

title: Single-cell multiome and live imaging of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC, or live reporters of FOS/JUN, to follow lineages and test whether the AP-1 state is inherited through divisions and is bistable. This separates heritable memory from transient signaling.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during memory maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 at different stages: before priming, during the rest period, and at restimulation. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, accessibility should persist after removal. If it is needed to maintain memory, accessibility and the faster secondary response should decay.

title: Sufficiency test with synthetic/optogenetic AP-1 activation and locus-specific editing
description: Induce AP-1 with optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN pulses of varied dose and duration, and use dCas9-based recruitment or motif mutation by CRISPR at selected enhancers. Test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to open chromatin and make a stable, restimulation-responsive state, and which sites need it.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined time windows
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of AP-1 components during the initial stimulus, during the memory (washout) phase, or during re-challenge. This separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it and from its role in executing the recall response.

title: Locus-specific causal editing of AP-1 motifs and chromatin state
description: Mutate or delete AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or recruit dCas9 effectors (writers/erasers of H3K27ac or DNA methylation) to them. Measure whether the primed state, and the enhanced re-response of nearby genes, depends on those sites and on partner pioneer factors or chromatin remodelers, such as SWI/SNF.

title: Time-windowed AP-1 inhibition (therapeutic window for memory)
description: Apply a selective AP-1 inhibitor (e.g., T-5224 or dominant-negative A-Fos) at defined windows: during priming only, during the rest period only, or during the challenge only. Run full concentration-response curves, and include inactive analogs and off-target controls for selectivity. If memory needs AP-1 during the rest period, it is maintained actively rather than just set at priming. The separation between memory-specific and acute-response IC50s defines the window.

title: Transient-stimulus hysteresis assay with chromatin accessibility readout
description: Expose cells to a defined, brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, or stress), wash out, and track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and ATAC-seq accessibility over days to weeks. Memory is supported if AP-1-dependent enhancers stay open and primed after TF levels return to baseline, and if a second challenge gives a faster or stronger transcriptional response than the first, which indicates path-dependence.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporters of AP-1 history
description: Pair scRNA/scATAC multiome with live imaging of AP-1 activity reporters or FOS-GFP knock-ins to track individual cells and their lineages. Test whether a cell's past AP-1 activity predicts its later accessibility and responsiveness, and whether this persists through cell divisions, which would show heritable memory beyond a population average.

title: Stimulus-memory chromatin accessibility time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) with a transient signal, then run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at multiple time points after washout. Persistent AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open after the signal ends, and that prime a faster or stronger response to restimulation, would support a memory role.

title: Targeted enhancer perturbation and sufficiency tests
description: Use CRISPR to delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin modifiers to test sufficiency, and use in vivo models (e.g., skin inflammatory memory, wound re-epithelialization) to ask whether motif-specific loss abolishes faster recall of the response. Together, these experiments separate AP-1 as a causal memory element from AP-1 binding that merely correlates with it.

title: Targeted motif editing and epigenome manipulation at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 factors or chromatin modifiers, and measure the effect on retained accessibility and faster re-induction of nearby genes. This tests sufficiency and necessity of AP-1 binding at individual loci for encoding memory, and extends to in vivo contexts such as wound-healing or immune-trained cells.

title: Re-stimulation response assay with single-cell readouts (primed vs. naive payoff)
description: Apply a first and second stimulus separated by variable delays, and measure the speed, amplitude, and cell-to-cell variability of transcriptional response (scRNA-seq, live reporters) versus naive cells. Fit decay kinetics of the primed advantage to estimate memory half-life, and test whether it depends on AP-1 dosage or motif integrity.

title: Inference of a landscape and dynamical model from single-cell data
description: Combine single-cell RNA-seq or multiome data with live reporters to fit a stochastic dynamical model, such as a Langevin or Fokker-Planck model, of AP-1 and its targets. Estimate the effective potential, the number of minima, barrier heights and Kramers-type switching rates. Then test the predictions: the model should forecast how memory lifetime scales with noise, feedback strength and AP-1 dosage, and those predictions can be checked experimentally.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 activity reporters in single cells through priming, rest and restimulation, and follow daughter cells. Correlate pulse history, dynamics and dimer composition with later responsiveness. This shows whether memory is stored in AP-1 levels, persistent feedback loops, or chromatin state that is inherited across divisions.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, stress) to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the signal and AP-1 levels have returned to baseline.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and sufficiency tests at AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPR deletion of AP-1 motifs or dCas9-based editing at memory enhancers, plus ectopic AP-1 induction, to test whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to establish lasting accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac), and enhanced re-induction, including pioneer-factor and BAF-complex dependence.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after memory has formed. If memory requires AP-1 only at establishment, the epigenetic state persists after removal. If memory requires AP-1 at maintenance, it decays.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of an AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, wounding cytokines, or inflammatory signals. Then run time-course ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for Fos/Jun, and H3K27ac after the stimulus is withdrawn, to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist for days to weeks after AP-1 activity returns to baseline.

title: Histone modification and chromatin remodeler co-profiling at AP-1 sites
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and BAF/SWI-SNF occupancy at AP-1 sites, and test whether inhibiting the remodeler or the modifying enzyme erases the memory. This tests whether AP-1 stores memory through epigenetic marks rather than its own continued presence.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and epigenome manipulation
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit or block chromatin modifiers there. Then measure the effect on persistent accessibility, histone marks, and the enhanced secondary response. This tests whether AP-1 binding at specific loci is causally required for memory, rather than merely correlated with it.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation (degron/dominant-negative) at different phases
description: Use an inducible degron or dominant-negative (e.g., A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the memory/maintenance phase. Distinguish AP-1 as an initiator of memory (needed only early) from a maintainer (needed continuously) by assessing chromatin state and re-challenge response.

title: Prime-rest-restimulate time course with chromatin profiling
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus (TPA, TNF, or wounding cues), let them rest for days to weeks, then restimulate. Measure ATAC-seq, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN, and RNA-seq to see whether primed cells show faster or stronger transcription and retained accessibility at AP-1 motif sites compared with naive cells.

title: Synthetic AP-1 induction sufficiency test with histone-mark readouts
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic pulses of FOS/JUN expression to ask if AP-1 alone is sufficient to create persistent enhancer accessibility and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 marks and memory-like responses. Pair with BAF/chromatin-remodeler inhibition to test the mechanism.

title: Optogenetic or synthetic AP-1 pulse-encoding experiments
description: Drive AP-1 with controlled pulses of different duration, frequency and amplitude, using optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN. Measure target-gene output and enhancer state after later challenges to determine whether AP-1 dynamics are integrated and stored, and whether the memory is dose- or timing-dependent.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use paired scRNA/scATAC-seq and live imaging of AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP knock-in, AP-1 motif reporters) to track whether individual cells retain heritable AP-1-linked accessibility states through divisions. Lineage tracing or sister-cell comparisons would distinguish true cell-autonomous, mitotically heritable memory from population-level selection or persistent paracrine signaling.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporters and dynamics imaging
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or AP-1 transcriptional reporters, with single-molecule tracking and optogenetic or pulsed stimulation. Quantify whether past stimulus history alters the amplitude, duration, or dimer composition of later AP-1 responses, and whether this predicts the memory state of single cells.

title: Locus-specific perturbation with dCas9 tools
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 motifs, plus CRISPR deletion/mutation of specific motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Check whether altering a single AP-1 site abolishes or creates memory at that gene (faster re-induction, retained accessibility) in cis, independent of global AP-1 levels.

title: Re-stimulation response assay with enhancer-level readouts
description: Prime cells, rest them, then restimulate and measure faster or stronger transcription (nascent RNA-seq such as PRO-seq, or scRNA-seq) at AP-1-bound loci versus unprimed controls. Pair this with H3K27ac and chromatin accessibility profiling to link a heightened response to AP-1-marked enhancers, and test whether AP-1 binding site mutation (CRISPR) removes the effect.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity dynamics
description: Track AP-1 activity using fluorescent reporters or tagged FOS/JUN in single cells over days and across divisions to measure persistence, bistability, and positive feedback (e.g., c-Jun autoregulation), and relate past activity history to current state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test necessity for maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/auxin) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after the stimulus has ended. Then measure whether memory accessibility and faster or stronger transcriptional re-induction on restimulation are lost. Removal during maintenance but not priming would show that AP-1 is needed to sustain memory, not only to establish it.

title: Channel capacity of the AP-1 write/read channel with and without chromatin feedback
description: Treat ERK/JNK dynamics as the input and AP-1 target-gene output (nascent RNA, enhancer accessibility) as the output, and estimate channel capacity from single-cell dose-response and dynamic-input distributions. Compare wild-type with perturbations (dominant-negative A-FOS, BAF/SWI-SNF inhibition, degron-tagged JUN) to show whether AP-1-dependent chromatin remodeling raises capacity or the number of distinguishable stored states beyond what transient transcription alone allows.

title: Acute degron-based AP-1 depletion at different time windows
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS, JUN or the pioneer-like AP-1 factors to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus, after it, or only during recall. If memory needs ongoing AP-1, removal after the priming phase should erase it. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, removal at that point should have no effect.

title: Motif mutation and synthetic enhancer tests with in vivo validation
description: Use CRISPR to edit or delete AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1/chromatin modifiers, and measure the effect on memory-associated accessibility and re-stimulation response. Complement with in vivo models such as epidermal wound or inflammation paradigms with lineage tracing to test relevance in tissue.

title: Secondary-stimulation transcriptional response assays
description: Compare RNA-seq (bulk and single-cell) of primed versus unprimed cells after a second challenge, and link faster or stronger induction of genes to AP-1-bound, pre-opened enhancers. Quantify memory with a response-ratio metric and test dependence on AP-1 motif integrity via CRISPR editing or MPRA of primed-state enhancers.

title: Re-stimulation (priming) assays with RNA-seq
description: Compare transcriptional responses in naive versus previously stimulated cells after a rest interval of varying length. Test whether faster or stronger induction of target genes depends on AP-1 levels and occupancy.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and epigenetic perturbation
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or dCas9-based writers or erasers (e.g., KRAB, p300, TET) to alter their chromatin state. Then test whether memory of the prior stimulus is lost or conferred. This establishes causal links between specific AP-1 sites, chromatin changes, and the memory phenotype, while controlling for cell cycle and for other transcription factors using cell-cycle-synchronized and parallel-lineage controls.

title: AP-1 family 'community composition' and diversity indices across time and cell states
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) and CUT&RUN or ChIP for each FOS/JUN/ATF member to quantify the relative abundance of AP-1 dimers at enhancers. Compute Shannon/Simpson diversity and beta-diversity (turnover) of AP-1 composition between naive, stimulated, and recovered cells to see whether a persistent compositional shift (a new stable community) marks memory.

title: Acute degron depletion of AP-1 during maintenance phase
description: Use an inducible degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) after the initiating stimulus has ended. If primed enhancers close and the enhanced secondary response is lost only when AP-1 is removed during the maintenance window, AP-1 is required for maintaining memory, not just establishing it.

title: Stimulus-history chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus such as TPA, serum, or LPS, then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at multiple times after washout and re-stimulation. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like imprint.

title: Primed re-stimulation response assays (memory phenotype)
description: Prime, rest, and re-stimulate cells, then compare transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) and kinetics of AP-1 target genes with naive cells. Test whether memory depends on AP-1 motifs by comparing wild-type with CRISPR-mutated motifs at selected enhancers, and by AP-1 inhibition during priming only.

title: Re-stimulation (priming) assays with transcriptional readouts
description: Compare primed and naive cells by RNA-seq or single-cell RNA-seq after a second stimulus given at varying intervals. Look for faster, stronger, or qualitatively different induction of AP-1 target genes in primed cells. The decay kinetics of this priming effect quantify how long the memory lasts.

title: Synergy analysis of AP-1 with co-regulators and epigenetic modifiers
description: Test combinations of AP-1 perturbation with inhibitors of chromatin regulators (BAF/SWI-SNF, p300, HDACs, DNMTs) in a dose-matrix. Analyze with Bliss and Loewe synergy models to see whether they act in the same pathway for memory maintenance. Synergy or antagonism patterns, plus Jun/Fos paralog-specific knockdown, help place AP-1 as an initiator, maintainer, or reader of memory.

title: Transient stimulus then washout: persistence of AP-1 chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating stimulus (TPA, TNF, injury), then withdraw it and track ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac at multiple time points. Persistent AP-1 motif-enriched accessible sites after signaling returns to baseline, and a faster or stronger transcriptional response to restimulation, would indicate memory.

title: Single-cell and lineage tracking of memory inheritance
description: Combine live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity or target genes with single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) and lineage barcoding to ask whether memory is carried through cell divisions and is heterogeneous across clones. Comparing sister cells, and the number of divisions after the stimulus, would show if memory is stable, heritable and cell-autonomous, versus a population-level or paracrine effect.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and FOS/JUN binding at multiple timepoints after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, or stress) and long after stimulus withdrawal. Persistent AP-1-motif-associated accessible sites would indicate a memory-like epigenetic state.

title: Positive-feedback and bistability test via synthetic circuits and mathematical modeling
description: Memory mechanisms predict hysteresis and self-sustaining states. Quantify AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels with live reporters across a dose-ramp up and down, and test for path dependence, bimodality, and decay time. Then cut candidate feedback edges, such as the JUN autoregulation promoter or the AP-1–BAF/p300 accessibility loop, in the DAG-informed model to see which edges are necessary for persistence. Fit competing models, including AP-1-independent ones like histone-mark memory, and compare them with held-out perturbations.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage-tracing of memory inheritance
description: Apply single-cell RNA plus ATAC (multiome) with barcode lineage tracing or live imaging of AP-1 reporters to follow primed cells through divisions. Test whether AP-1 occupancy or accessibility is inherited by daughter cells and whether it predicts clonal differences in later responses. This separates heritable memory from persistent signaling, and shows how stable it is across cell cycles.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), let signaling return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility against naive cells to test whether prior exposure leaves a lasting, AP-1-dependent change in response.

title: Comparative evolutionary analysis of AP-1 memory sites across species and cell types
description: Compare AP-1-primed enhancers across mammals or other lineages with ATAC, ChIP and conservation scores, and test whether motif turnover and constraint are stronger at sites showing memory than at sites showing transient responses. Add population-level variant data (eQTL/caQTL) to test whether memory-linked elements are under purifying selection, which would show that memory has fitness value. Examine trade-offs such as faster re-response against the cost of maladaptive persistence in chronic inflammation or cancer.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage-tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use single-cell RNA plus ATAC, with barcoded lineage tracing, to follow stimulated cells and their daughters through divisions. Quantify whether sister cells share AP-1 target accessibility and expression more than unrelated cells. Combine with live imaging of AP-1 reporters to check for heritable states that persist through mitosis.

title: Synthetic sufficiency test with optogenetic or CRISPR-targeted AP-1 sites
description: Pulse AP-1 activity with optogenetic FOS/JUN, or use dCas9-based recruitment or deletion of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers. Then measure whether accessibility, pioneer-factor cooperation (e.g., with BAF), and gene responsiveness persist after the pulse, testing sufficiency and locus-specific necessity.

title: Targeted synthetic perturbation of AP-1 sites at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion of AP-1 motifs, together with dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 at specific enhancers. Test whether memory at a given gene needs local AP-1 binding, and whether forced AP-1 occupancy alone is enough to create memory without a prior stimulus. Add measurements of nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment) and histone marks to define the mechanism.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative block during priming versus recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the initial priming stimulus or only during the later restimulation. If depletion at priming abolishes the enhanced secondary response but depletion at recall does not, AP-1 is needed to write the memory rather than just to read it.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (TPA, TNF, wounding, or stress). Then run time-course ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS, H3K27ac, and H3K4me1 after washout, to test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and occupied well after the stimulus and AP-1 activity have returned to baseline.
